title: P0 Hosted API: Autoscaler hysteresis regression causing capacity undershoot and streaming 5xxs
content:
Summary:

On 2029-04-03 between 09:18 UTC and 10:10 UTC the Hosted API experienced a P0 degradation: p95/p99 latency spiked to values 3–8x above SLO, and a subset of streaming sessions returned 5xx errors. The incident lasted ~52 minutes from first alert to rollback of a config change. Root cause was a regression in the autoscaler hysteresis parameters combined with a slow-path in the scale-up decision that delayed capacity provisioning during a sustained traffic ramp. The temporary capacity undershoot triggered queueing, KV cache coldstarts, and memory pressure on a small number of worker pods that then crashed with OOMs producing 5xx responses.

Impact:
- Duration: ~09:18 to ~10:10 UTC (alerts started 09:18, mitigation rollback at 10:05, full recovery by 10:10).
- Affected surface: Hosted API - streaming and non-streaming generation endpoints in us-west-2.
- Customer impact: ~2.2% of token generation requests observed elevated latency; ~0.3% returned 5xx. Several paying customers reported degraded user experience and filed support tickets.
- SRE/Eng time: multi-team pagers engaged for ~1.5 hours including on-call, serving-runtime, and infra owners.

What happened (high level):
1) At 09:06 UTC a configuration change (PR 1842) was merged that altered autoscaler hysteresis and smoothing parameters intended to reduce transient oscillation during noisy workloads. The change increased the EMA smoothing window from ~3m to ~8m and lengthened the scale-down stabilization window.
2) Traffic pattern at 09:15 UTC started a sustained ramp (gradual increase over 8 minutes) due to a customer marketing event. The smoothed metric used by the autoscaler did not reflect the real-time increase fast enough because of the larger smoothing window. Meanwhile, a separate bug in the downward scaling logic caused a small cluster of nodes to be removed prematurely during an earlier short dip (this bug had low probability but was present).
3) At ~09:18 autoscaler decisions left us with fewer worker replicas than required for the incoming rate (undershoot). Queues started to grow, p95 and p99 latencies rose as requests waited for available inference slots and the KV cache suffered higher miss rates (cold starts).
4) Increased memory pressure from concurrent cache misses and request contention caused a few worker processes to exceed memory limits and crash with OOM, producing 5xxs for those sessions. Hedge/replica fallbacks were insufficient because the fallbacks were rate-limited to avoid amplification and did not trigger fast enough.

Timeline (abridged):
- 09:06 UTC: infra PR 1842 merged (autoscaler smoothing increase + scale-down stabilization).
- 09:12 UTC: automated canary checks passed (did not cover aggressive ramp scenarios).
- 09:15 UTC: production traffic begins sustained ramp (marketing-driven).
- 09:18 UTC: first pager alert - p95 latency exceeded alert threshold; SRE on-call pages.
- 09:23 UTC: SREs observe queued requests rising in the edge/acceptor layer; serving-runtime team notified.
- 09:30 UTC: evidence of underprovisioned pods in us-west-2; attempts to manually force scale show limited immediate effect due to slow node provisioning in the protected pool.
- 09:42 UTC: two worker pods OOM and restart loops observed; 5xx spike correlates.
- 09:55 UTC: mitigation decision to rollback PR 1842 and revert autoscaler hysteresis to previous parameters. Rollback initiated.
- 10:05 UTC: autoscaler behavior reverts; scale-up completes and queued work drains.
- 10:10 UTC: p95/p99 return to baseline; incident declared mitigated.

Root cause analysis:
Primary root cause: A configuration regression (PR 1842) increased autoscaler smoothing and stabilization windows in a way that delayed scale-up decisions during valid sustained ramps. This made the system slow to react to real load increases and created capacity undershoot.
Contributing factors:
- A low-probability bug in the scale-down path removed a small number of nodes during a transient dip. When combined with the slower scale-up, this resulted in a net deficit.
- Canary tests and pre-merge checks did not simulate the specific ramp-shaped traffic pattern. Current canaries emphasize oscillation prevention rather than fast ramp detection.
- Hedge/fallback throttles were tuned conservatively to prevent amplification; they did not provide the intended protection under this combined failure mode.

Detection and monitoring gaps:
- Alerts fired only after p95 latency breached thresholds; there was no early alert on queue depth or active pending requests that would have signaled capacity friction earlier.
- Autoscaler decision telemetry (raw metric vs smoothed metric) was not visible in a single dashboard for quick triage. Engineers had to stitch logs to prove the smoothing lag.

Mitigation and remediation performed during the incident:
- Immediate rollback of PR 1842 to restore previous hysteresis and smoothing parameters (10:05 UTC).
- Temporary increase of pod memory limits on the affected node pool to reduce OOM risk while nodes came back up (rolled back after recovery).
- Manual scale-up attempts and prioritization of node provisioning for the affected pool.

Longer-term fixes and action items (owner, due date):
1) Autoscaler fast-ramp path: add explicit fast-path detection for sustained increases (if rate increases > X% over Y seconds) that can temporarily bypass long smoothing windows for scale-up decisions. Owner: Jamal Rivera. Due: 2029-04-17.
2) Rework PR 1842: revert commit in prod (done) and create follow-up that parameterizes smoothing by workload class and adds an explicit canary for ramp tests. Owner: Priya Nair. Due: 2029-04-10.
3) Fix scale-down bug found in codepath (low probability, high impact). Owner: Liam O'Donnell. Due: 2029-04-12.
4) Add early-warning alerts: queue depth > 200 for 30s, pending requests > 5% of capacity for 60s. Owner: Maya Chen. Due: 2029-04-09.
5) Dashboard: single pane showing raw metric, smoothed metric, autoscaler decision, and pending queue length to accelerate triage. Owner: Serving-runtime observability. Due: 2029-04-16.
6) Hedge fallback tuning: create an automated escalation that temporarily relaxes rate-limiting on replica fallbacks when autoscaler is in a scale-up-required state. Owner: Runtime team. Due: 2029-04-24.
7) Chaos/canary expansion: add synthetic ramp-shaped traffic tests as part of pre-merge CI for autoscaler changes. Owner: Release engineering + Infra. Due: 2029-05-01.

Runbook changes (immediate):
- Add a new checklist under "Hosted API - capacity emergencies" titled "Autoscaler hysteresis regression" with steps: (1) check pending queue depth, (2) inspect raw metric vs smoothed metric, (3) if smoothed metric lags and capacity deficit present -> consider manual scale or rollback parameter change, (4) temporarily relax fallback throttles, (5) notify infra to prioritize node provisioning.
- Add explicit runbook section for "fast ramp" scenarios with thresholds and who to page (platform-scheduling, serving-runtime).

Post-incident notes and learnings:
- Hysteresis/smoothing tradeoffs are workload dependent; a one-size-fits-all parameterization is fragile. We need workload-specific profiles or an adaptive approach.
- Canary suites must include sustained ramp shapes, not only oscillatory noise tests.
- Observable signals that couple autoscaler decisions with queue depth and fallback health dramatically reduce time-to-diagnosis.

Customer communication:
- Support drafted a proactive notice to affected customers (sent 2029-04-04) explaining the incident, mitigation, and actions taken. Customer Success scheduled follow-up calls for any enterprise customers who saw degraded UX.

Appendix: quick artifacts for triage
- Linear ticket: SRE-4921 (incident timeline + logs)
- Infra PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/infra/pull/1842 (reverted)
- Slack incident thread: https://redwood.slack.com/archives/C01SRE/threads/p0-autoscaler-2029-04-03

Open questions:
- Can we automatically detect 'marketing-style' ramps (many customers but similar request per-customer) vs organic growth to pick scaling profiles?
- What guardrails can we add to prevent combined low-probability bugs (scale-down bug) from amplifying config changes?

If you were on-call for this incident and have additional notes or logs that might help the RCA, paste them into the Slack thread and add to SRE-4921.
